strategy.angle: The geopolitical and infrastructure shift of AI compute landing in Texas.
strategy.audience: Houston business leaders, CEOs, and infrastructure stakeholders.

draft.hook: Silicon Valley is no longer just shipping software; they are terraforming the Texas landscape to house the engine of the next decade.
draft.body: OpenAI’s formal outreach to Governor Abbott isn't just about 'responsible AI'—it’s a direct move to secure the Lone Star State as the primary compute hub for global model training. Why is Texas the target? Because AI at scale is a game of physics, not just code. You need three things: massive, reliable power grids, affordable land, and sustainable water for cooling. Houston’s energy sector leaders at Amplify Intelligence have been tracking this shift closely; we estimate that AI infrastructure requirements will increase regional power demand by 15-20% by 2027. This transition moves AI from a 'technology investment' to a core component of the state’s industrial infrastructure. Is this shift purely beneficial? For the Texas economy, it represents a massive influx of capital, but it creates a zero-sum game for local power resources and water allocation. We are looking at a future where your competitive advantage in Houston won't just depend on your software stack, but on your proximity to the underlying grid capacity that OpenAI and its peers are currently monopolizing.
draft.closing: Leon Coe and the team at Amplify Intelligence are currently advising regional stakeholders on how to navigate this infrastructure collision before it shifts from a strategic advantage to an operational bottleneck.
draft.cta: If your firm is currently planning a five-year capital budget, how much of that is allocated to energy resilience in an AI-saturated market?
